content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank You for your review of the paper. We address your concerns below:

1. **Information about Generalized and Zero Shot Setting**: Thanks for pointing this out. We have added details about the two at the start of the Methodology Section. To reiterate the same here, in Zero-Shot setting, training is done on (set of seen labels, document) pairs, and during evaluation predictions are made only on labels unseen at train time. The training procedure is the same for Generalized ZeroShot, however evaluation is done on the combined set of seen and unseen labels.

2. **Improvement with Soft Lexical Matching over COIL**: Thanks for pointing this out. We have mentioned in the ablations the improvement of soft lexical matching is 2.4 P@1 points on Eurlex and 3.7 P@1 points on Amazon dataset. This is a significant improvement in this setting, and therefore we believe this is a valuable contribution in this field . Also, we have updated the design of the ablation table to make it more clear. 

3. **Comparison with other Information Retrieval methods**: 
We have run the Splade model (we try different variants and exact details are in Appendix A.2), and find that the numbers are significantly lower in zero-shot setting when compared to SemSup-XC(19.5 P@1 points for Amazon dataset). We argue that XC is significantly different from IR, because of multi-label problems, lack of concrete query-document format and tail distribution in XC. Thus naively applying IR methods in XC doesn’t perform good, and suitable changes such as higher sampling rate(instead of in-batch negatives), providing rich label features is necessary in XC. 
Here is the performance comparison of Splade with our method: 
| Model     | P@1 (Eurlex - ZS) | P@1 (Amzn - ZS) | P@1 (Wiki - ZS) |
|-----------|-------------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| SemSup-XC | 49.7              | 48.5            | 36.5            |
| Splade    | 20.2              | 17.2            | 14.3            |

4. **Efficiency Related to Contextualized Token Embeddings**: 
Thanks for pointing this out. We have added the details of efficiency in the appendix in the revised paper. Our method doesn’t have high memory or storage requirements in terms of XC standards. This is because unlike Information Retrieval, we tokenize the label descriptions which have average length of around 128 instead of the long documents in Information Retrieval. Moreover, the dimension of token embeddings is kept at 16, thus overall despite storing embeddings of 1.3M labels (as in Wikipedia), our method requires 18 GB of total storage. 
Here is the efficiency table that we included in the revised paper: 
| Model     | Throughput (Inputs/s) | Storage (GB) | P@1 (Wiki-ZSL) |
|-----------|-----------------------|--------------|----------------|
| SemSup-XC | 46.2                  | 17.9         | 36.5           |
| MACLR     | 77.8                  | 4.6          | 29.8           |
| GROOV     | 8.9                   | 0.4          | 6.0            |


Once again, thank you for the review. We hope your concerns were clarified by the above points. We will be happy to address any of the other concerns that you may have.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable review of the paper. We address your concerns below:
1. **Novelty and Contributions of SemSup-XC**: We believe that we make several technical contributions. 1) We adapt SemSup, which is very computationally inefficient and performs poorly on extreme classification (XC) by including contrastive learning. Even naively applying contrastive learning is not feasible, and efficient mining of hard negatives is necessary(eg: with random sampling, we get deterioration of ~30 P@1 points in Wikipedia dataset). 2) We propose a soft lexical matching model based on COIL which outperforms all state-of-the-art baselines. (Soft matching improves P@1 scores by 3.7 on Amazon Dataset) 3) We provide a scalable way to collect descriptions for label spaces as large as a million, where labels are often extremely fine-grained(eg: ‘Fencers at the 1984 Summer Olympics’ is a label in Wikipedia dataset)
2. **Importance of Label Descriptions**: The label descriptions scraped provide definition semantic information to the labels, and not the input associated with the label. Thus we claim that label descriptions should not be considered as a data hack, but rather a means to provide information about the labels to the model. For example consider the label: ‘Fencers at the 1984 Summer Olympics’ from Wikipedia dataset. Our method ensemble the descriptions of constituents (viz. Fencers, 1984, Summer Olympics) of label name, providing a rich semantic information to model about the whole label. 
3. **Comparison and Performance of Baselines in Table 2**: \
a. Thanks for the suggestions and questions. We have included baselines run both with and without web descriptions in table 2. The trends remain the same, with our model significantly outperforming other state-of-the art methods. \
b. Thanks for mentioning about the performance of TF-IDF. We have made the reason for good performance more explicit in Section 5.1. \
c. The high performance is due to the fact that sparse retrievers often perform better than dense methods in out-of-domain tasks and zero-shot settings [1]. This is because dense methods are often unable to extract and match fine-grained information and new entities[2].
4. **Performance of Bi-encoders with descriptions**: Our ablation with removal of exact lexical matching is technically equivalent to bi-encoder. We see that the scores are significantly lower for both Eurlex(31 P@1 lower) and Amazon(11 P@1 lower) datasets, when compared to our method. This shows that the suggested changes in architecture and inclusion of descriptions are both important for good performance of our method. We present the ablation numbers here as well for convenience.
5. **Releasing Web Scraped Descriptions and CodeBase**: Thank You for pointing this out. We have uploaded the web-scraped descriptions in the code submitted in supplementary material. Also for reproducibility, the code contains all training and evaluation scripts and configs for SemSup-XC and all baselines. Further, we have provided links to pretrained models in each case. Thus, code can be easily used to ensure reproducibility.
6. **Ablation on Performance Gain**: In section 5.3, we have mentioned the scores by removing web descriptions and architectural changes from our method. Effectively, both the descriptions and architectural changes are important, since with inclusion of descriptions we get 4.4P@1 improvement in Amazon, and 11.4P@1 points by making the architectural changes. This reiterates the importance of our suggested changes in terms of both architecture and descriptions. 


Once again, thank you for the review. We hope your concerns were clarified by the above points. We will be happy to address any of the other concerns that you may have.

References:
1. Thakur, N., Reimers, N., Ruckl'e, A., Srivastava, A., & Gurevych, I. (2021). BEIR: A Heterogenous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models. ArXiv, abs/2104.08663.
2. Chen, X., Lakhotia, K., Oğuz, B., Gupta, A., Lewis, P., Peshterliev, S., Mehdad, Y., Gupta, S., & Yih, W. (2021). Salient Phrase Aware Dense Retrieval: Can a Dense Retriever Imitate a Sparse One? ArXiv, abs/2110.06918.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths :
1. The paper addresses an important problem which is gaining more traction within the domain of extreme classification, and approach seems quite reasonable. 

2. The experimental results are quite good, and significant improvement over state-of-the-art is demonstrated. However, for an experimental paper, it would have been better if the code was also provided.

Weaknesses :

1. The novelty in the paper seems rather limited, as it is based on the earlier works, SEMSUP, and COIL for similarity matching. The improvements for scaling to extreme classification (i) contrastive learning with negative sampling, and (ii) soft lexical matching in equation (5), relaxed-coil, are somewhat standard.

It jumps straight into the Semantic Supervision, and ignoring the zero-shot extreme classification setup. I think it is important to describe the problem setup precisely to not confuse with other XMC settings such as long/short text, with or without label features, what part of training/test data is available etc.

An ablation could include replacing the label description, which are sourced externally,  by label texts only as in MACLR. Also, I am a bit unclear about the nearest neighbor results with sparse tf-idf data representation. Typically, nearest neighbor with sparse data has not been very promising.
4. It seems that the inference can be slow that for an unseen label, the description needs to be fetched by search the web. This part is missing in the paper, and no inference timings/comparisons are given. 
5. The paper could also benefit from more detailed literature review of various existing extreme classification settings, and positioning itself accordingly.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors propose a new algorithm for extreme zero/few-shot multi-label classification. The algorithm is an extension of the SEMSUP (Hanjie et al., 2022) algorithm previously introduced for the task of zero/few-shot learning, in which the main idea is to estimate a conditional probability of the label as a product of instances embedding (produced by a decoder, here BERT decoder) and label description embedding (produced by the second decoder) passed through sigmoid function. There are three main changes introduced in this work:
1) application of the popular technique of negative sampling to improve the computational performance of the algorithm,
2) addition of a soft lexico-semantic similarity model, similar to COIL (Gao et al., 2021b),
3) introduction of the protocol for scrapping search engine results to obtain labels description on which the algorithm relies.

The modified algorithm is named SEMSUP-XC and it's empirically compared with some simple unsupervised baselines, as well as 3 recently introduced algorithms for zero-shot learning in the extreme classification setting on 3 datasets. The proposed approach outperforms other algorithms on both zero-shot and few-shot learning tasks. The authors also provide an ablation study of introduced modifications.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
+ The proposed method significantly outperforms other algorithms considered in the comparison on unseen labels.
+ The ablation study is a nice addition in the context of extending the SEMSUP algorithm.

Weaknesses:
- The modifications to the SEMSUM algorithms are minor.
- Vague descriptions in many places, especially in the experimental section, that force a reader to guess what the method is.
- The introduced method uses auxiliary information, while other methods, if I remember correctly, rely only on label names and don't use data not included in the benchmark. We can also see that scrapping a web for additional description is similar to using other sources to generate some new instances with labels for the problem. I think that for few-shot learning, including scrapped descriptions as learning examples for other methods would be a more fair comparison.
- While during training, the negative sampling is used to speed-up training, there is no description of inference. I assume it's performed in linear time by calculating scores for all the labels. Since inference performance is important for XMLC, comment on that and how to speed up inference in the case of this method would be a great addition.
- The authors mention they utilize labels hierarchy, it's impact is also shown in the ablation study, but I don't see a clear description of how it is used in the paper. Is the label description generated by adding the names of parent labels?
- The authors include the addition of web-scraped descriptions in the ablation study, but it is not clear what the variant is without them. What is the description in this case? Just a name of the class? The name of the label and its parents, if the hierarchy is available?
- It's not entirely clear how T5 and Sentence Transformer baselines work. I guess they use the nearest neighbor between embedding of the instance and labels' descriptions, as in the case of tf-idf baseline?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity and quality: Not all details are clear from the text.

Novelty: I find the paper not very novel. Introduce method is minor modifications to the SEMSUP algorithm (which is also simple) to adjust it for the setting of extreme zero/few-shot learning classification.

Reproducibility: The paper doesn't consist of all the necessary details to guarantee the reproducibility of the results. On top of the lack of details in the method description, there is also very little information about dataset creation and hyperparameters.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Despite some interesting empirical results, I find the paper lacking, at least in novelty and clarity. Because of that, I recommend the rejection of the paper.

---

**After the authors' responses:**
I thank the authors for their response to my review. The authors addressed some of my and other reviewers' concerns, mostly improving the clarity of experimental comparison by providing important details, providing results for more variants of baseline algorithms and their proposed method (better ablation study), and adding code. The new results suggest that web-scrapped descriptions are far less important than the use of hierarchy to generate descriptions, which makes the reviewers' comments about the unfairness of comparison a little less critical. However, the novelty remains the main concern of this work as the proposed method is very similar to SEMSUP and COIL. I'm raising my score to marginally below the acceptance threshold.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable review of the paper! We address your concerns below:

1. **Modifications from SemSup to SemSup-XC**: 
Naively applying SemSup algorithm to extreme classification (XC) settings is both computationally infeasible and performs worse (eg: almost 33 P@1 points in Eurlex dataset). In terms of computational feasibility, SemSup is slow even for small datasets in XC. Further our experiments suggested naively applying contrastive learning is not feasible, and models trained without hard negatives results in much poorer scores (eg: ~30 P@1 points in Wikipedia dataset). In terms of architectural changes, we improve COIL based architecture by including soft lexical matching, which results in 2.4 and 3.7 P@1 increase in points on Eurlex and Amazon datasets. Moreover, naively scraping for descriptions is not feasible for Extreme classification, due to the nature of fine grained labels, simple search results don’t result in helpful information. We have proposed changes to SemSup that enable collecting high-quality descriptions of common labels and also for very fine-grained labels by collecting descriptions of separate constituents of labels and applying proper processing on them. We refer you to the appendix B in the revision paper for more details. We thus believe the modifications to SemSup are significant.  

2. **Clarity in the experimental section**: 
Thank you for pointing this out. We have added more details in the experimental section to make the methods clearer. Specifically, we elaborate on methodology of baselines, and refer Appendix A.2 to provide exact details on dataset splits, baselines and SemSup-XC

3. **Use of auxiliary information in baselines**:
a. We have updated the table in paper to include both variants of all baselines: 1.) With descriptions 2.) Without descriptions. Both variants use hierarchy. \
b. For the ease of reading, we include part of main table for Wikipedia dataset here: \
| Model                     | P@1 (ZS) | P@1 (GZS) |
|---------------------------|----------|-----------|
| MACLR w/o descriptions    | 28.6     | 26.7      |
| MACLR with descriptions   | 30.7     | 28.1      |
| ZestXML w/o descriptions  | 15.8     | 26.3      |
| ZestXML with descriptions | 10.6     | 20.9      |
| SemSup-XC                 | 36.5     | 33.7      |
c. Inclusion of description has little to no effect on baselines. They require the right choice of architecture for them to be utilized properly. Thus SemSup-XC takes advantage of both web descriptions and architectural improvements resulting in much better performance. 
4. **Analysis of Inference Time**: 
a. We have updated the manuscript to include efficiency metrics(Section 6). \
b. Our model is as efficient as other methods. Here is the relevant part of efficiency table: 
| Model     | Throughput (Inputs/s) |
|-----------|-----------------------|
| SemSup-XC | 46.2                  |
| MACLR     | 77.8                  |
| GROOV     | 8.9                   |
c. At inference, our model ranks among the top 1000 labels shortlisted using TF-IDF scores, just as it did during training. As a result, our method is computationally efficient in terms of speed when compared to other state-of-the-art baselines. 

5. **Utilization and Construction of Label Hierarchy**:
a. We have added information about the general structure of label hierarchy along with an example in the appendix. \
b. To reiterate it here, Label Hierarchy consists of alternate names, parents, children. For each label, we restructure the label hierarchy (present in the dataset) of the label in a natural language format and pass it to the output encoder.  \
c. An example of Label Hierarchy for label `video surveillance` is: \
`Label is video surveillance.\nDescription is <web_scraped_description>.\nParents are video communications.\nAlternate Label Names are camera surveillance, security camera surveillance.’` \
 The whole text is passed to the output encoder. 
6. **Analysis of web-scraped descriptions in the ablation study**:
 We have updated the table to make it clearer what each of the variants contains. Specifically, the second row of Table 3, uses hierarchy and class names(instead of web descriptions). For convenience, here is the part of ablation table concerned with label descriptions
 | Model                         | P@1 (ZS) | R@10 (ZS) | P@1 (GZS) | R@10 (GZS) |

content.title: Response - Contd.
content.comment:
7. **Working of Baselines**: We have added text in Section 4 to make the working of Sentence Transformer and T5 more explicit, and also mentioned more details for other baselines in the appendix. For Sentence Transformer, similarity between the input and embeddings is compared(similar to tf-idf baseline). T5 is evaluated as an NLI task and labels are ranked based on the likelihood of entailment. 
8. **Reproducibility of Scores and Codebase**: We have uploaded the code in supplementary material containing all training and evaluation scripts and configs for SemSup-XC and all baselines. Further, we have provided links to pretrained models in each case. The code can be easily used to ensure reproducibility. 
9. **Information about Dataset Creation and Hyperparameters**:
 We had provided the details in the appendix section, and have elaborated more on them in the revised paper and appendix. To reiterate, for creating splits we use the same method as mentioned in GROOV. Effectively, we sample 50% of the labels in the train dataset, and mark them unseen, i.e they are not trained on. We tune our hyperparameters on the validation set on Eurlex. Similar to other XC methods, we keep the hyperparameters the same on other datasets. 

Once again, thank you for your response. We hope the comment clarifies all of your concerns. We will be happy to address any of the other concerns that you may have.
